title: Reading Results Like a Detective: Paired Clues in Azotemia, the Adrenal Axis and COPD Oxygen
summary: Read three classic result pairs with their limits: the cortisol–ACTH grid for adrenal insufficiency and Cushing syndrome, why the BUN/creatinine ratio is only a weak hint of prerenal injury, and controlled oxygen to 88–92% for COPD patients at risk of hypercapnia.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 9 Hits 4, 9 and 10 and Trap 6. Checked against Uchino 2012, Manoeuvrier 2017, Lewis 2023, Savas 2022, BTS 2017 (O’Driscoll) and Abdo 2012 (full texts read via Europe PMC). Hit 4’s ratio rule (>20:1 prerenal; 10–20:1 intrinsic) is contradicted (register flag rv-bun-cr-ratio-ch9; the Ch. 15 flag rv-bun-cr-ratio-prerenal covers the same claim there). Hit 9’s “high + high = Cushing disease” is qualified (rv-acth-dependent-ch9). Hit 10/Trap 6 agree with BTS; the 94–98% adjustment when PCO₂ is normal is added (rv-copd-o2-target-adjust-ch9). Not taught: Number Vault (table1), diabetes cut-offs, troponin kinetics, cortisol reference values.

objectives: Classify cortisol–ACTH pairs into primary or secondary adrenal insufficiency and ACTH-independent or ACTH-dependent Cushing syndrome.
Explain why a BUN/creatinine ratio above 20 does not reliably separate prerenal from intrinsic acute kidney injury, and list non-renal influences on BUN.
State the BTS oxygen targets for patients with and without risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure, and the main mechanisms of oxygen-induced hypercapnia.

scenes.title: Three paired clues
scenes.altText: Invented scenario. Three emergency patients, each with a pair of results: (1) BUN 60 mg/dL with creatinine 2.0 mg/dL (ratio 30) after days of vomiting; (2) a low morning cortisol with a high ACTH in a tired, hyperpigmented patient; (3) a COPD exacerbation with SpO₂ 84% on room air and a history of hypercapnia. Question token: “What does each pair prove — and what doesn’t it?”

cues.text: Three emergency patients, each with a pair of clues. First: a urea nitrogen of sixty and a creatinine of two after days of vomiting, a ratio of thirty.
Second: a low morning cortisol with a high ACTH in a tired patient with darkened skin. Third: a COPD flare with an oxygen saturation of eighty-four percent and a history of carbon dioxide retention.
What does each pair really prove, and what does it not?

scenes.title: How the pairs are supposed to work
scenes.altText: Rule cards. Axis card (Lewis 2023): hypothalamic CRH → pituitary ACTH → adrenal cortisol, with negative feedback from cortisol; primary adrenal insufficiency = failure of the adrenal gland itself, secondary = lack of ACTH or CRH stimulation. Ratio card (Uchino 2012; Manoeuvrier 2017): the traditional theory is that in renal hypoperfusion antidiuretic hormone increases reabsorption of water and urea, so BUN rises out of proportion to creatinine, with a traditional cut-off of 20. Oxygen card (BTS 2017): target SpO₂ 94–98% for most acutely ill patients; 88–92% for those at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure, pending blood gases.

cues.text: Cortisol sits at the bottom of a chain: the hypothalamus releases CRH, the pituitary releases ACTH, and the adrenal cortex makes cortisol, which then feeds back to switch the chain down.
So the adrenal gland itself can fail, which is primary adrenal insufficiency, or the ACTH or CRH signal can fail, which is secondary.

The urea nitrogen to creatinine ratio rests on a theory: with poor kidney perfusion, antidiuretic hormone makes the tubules reabsorb water and urea, so urea rises more than creatinine. The traditional cut-off is twenty.

And oxygen has targets. For most acutely ill adults, the British Thoracic Society aims for saturations of ninety-four to ninety-eight percent. For those at risk of carbon dioxide retention, eighty-eight to ninety-two percent until blood gases are back.

scenes.title: The cortisol–ACTH grid
scenes.altText: Four-quadrant grid. Low cortisol + raised ACTH = primary adrenal insufficiency (Lewis 2023: a low baseline cortisol with raised ACTH can be enough to diagnose it; autoimmune adrenalitis >70% of cases in the Western world; hyperpigmentation only in primary). Low cortisol + low ACTH = secondary adrenal insufficiency (pituitary or hypothalamic; exogenous glucocorticoids suggested as the most common cause). High cortisol + low ACTH (generally <10 pg/mL) = ACTH-independent (adrenal) Cushing syndrome, 15–20% of endogenous cases (Savas 2022). High cortisol + inappropriately normal or elevated ACTH (generally >20 pg/mL) = ACTH-dependent, 80–85%: Cushing disease (pituitary adenoma, ~80% of ACTH-dependent) or ectopic ACTH (e.g. small-cell lung carcinoma, pulmonary carcinoid). ACTH 5–20 pg/mL is a gray zone. The most common cause of Cushing syndrome overall is exogenous corticosteroids.

cues.text: Low cortisol with a raised ACTH: the pituitary is shouting at an adrenal gland that cannot answer. That is primary adrenal insufficiency, in Western countries most often autoimmune, and only this form darkens the skin.

Low cortisol with a low ACTH: the signal itself is missing. That is secondary adrenal insufficiency, from the pituitary or hypothalamus, and prescribed glucocorticoids are thought to be its most common cause.

High cortisol with a suppressed ACTH, generally below ten picograms per millilitre: the adrenal is making cortisol on its own. That is ACTH-independent Cushing syndrome, about fifteen to twenty percent of endogenous cases.

High cortisol with an ACTH that is normal or high: ACTH-dependent, about eighty to eighty-five percent. Most is Cushing disease from a pituitary adenoma, the rest ectopic ACTH, for example from lung tumours. Values between five and twenty sit in a gray zone.

scenes.title: Testing the ratio and the oxygen story
scenes.altText: Evidence cards. Uchino 2012 (3641 inpatients with AKI): 53.2% had a ratio >20; the distribution was not bimodal; a high ratio carried HIGHER hospital mortality (29.9% vs 18.4%), the opposite of what a benign prerenal state predicts; the authors conclude the ratio cannot be justified for separating prerenal azotemia from ATN. Manoeuvrier 2017 (1103 emergency patients): no significant difference in mean ratio between prerenal and intrinsic AKI; ROC area 0.5. Non-renal influences: GI bleeding, high protein intake, catabolism (fever, trauma, infection), corticosteroids and tetracycline raise the ratio; liver failure, protein malnutrition, osmotic diuresis and acetazolamide lower it. Oxygen card (Abdo 2012): oxygen-induced hypercapnia comes mostly from worsened V/Q matching as oxygen releases hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction, then the Haldane effect (about a quarter in the cited study); reduced respiratory drive is a minor contributor.

cues.text: Test the ratio. In over three thousand hospital patients with acute kidney injury, about half had a ratio above twenty, the values formed one continuous spread, and a high ratio carried higher, not lower, mortality.
In over a thousand emergency patients, the average ratio did not differ between prerenal and intrinsic injury. The area under the curve was zero point five, no better than a coin toss.
Why? Urea moves for reasons outside the kidney. Gut bleeding, a high protein load, fever, trauma and steroids push it up. Liver failure and malnutrition pull it down.
Now the oxygen story. Too much oxygen raises carbon dioxide mainly by worsening the match of air and blood flow in the lung, plus the Haldane effect. Loss of breathing drive plays only a small part.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “A ratio of 30 proves prerenal azotemia” (✓ a weak hint at most; the ratio does not separate prerenal from intrinsic AKI, and bleeding, protein and catabolism raise it); “Hypercapnic COPD: hold the oxygen” (✓ give controlled oxygen, 24% or 28% Venturi, target 88–92%, blood gases within 30–60 min; never stop oxygen abruptly); “High cortisol + high ACTH = Cushing disease” (✓ ACTH-dependent: pituitary Cushing disease OR ectopic ACTH, and ACTH may be only inappropriately normal).

cues.text: Trap one: a ratio of thirty proves prerenal azotemia. No: the ratio does not reliably separate prerenal from intrinsic injury, and bleeding or catabolism can raise it.
Trap two: a COPD patient who retains carbon dioxide should get no oxygen. No: give controlled oxygen to eighty-eight to ninety-two percent and check blood gases within thirty to sixty minutes.
Trap three: high cortisol with high ACTH is always Cushing disease. No: it is ACTH-dependent, from the pituitary or an ectopic tumour, and the ACTH may only be inappropriately normal.

scenes.title: Furnace, thermostat, dimmer, rumour
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “When the FURNACE (adrenal) breaks, the THERMOSTAT (pituitary ACTH) shouts louder; when the thermostat breaks, both go quiet. A furnace running on its own silences the thermostat. Oxygen is a DIMMER, not an on-off switch: dial it to 88–92. And the BUN/creatinine ratio is a RUMOUR, not a witness.” Tokens: furnace broken = ACTH high · dimmer 88–92 · ratio = rumour. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: when the furnace, the adrenal, breaks, the thermostat, ACTH, shouts louder. When the thermostat breaks, both go quiet. Oxygen is a dimmer, not an on-off switch. And the ratio is a rumour, not a witness.

Where it breaks: ACTH can sit in a gray zone; severe illness and stress change how cortisol should be read; and the oxygen target moves to ninety-four to ninety-eight percent if blood gases show normal carbon dioxide and no past hypercapnic failure.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Cortisol ↓ + ACTH ↑ = primary · ↓ + ↓ = secondary · cortisol ↑ + ACTH ↓ = adrenal · cortisol ↑ + ACTH normal/↑ = pituitary or ectopic”, “BUN/creatinine ratio = weak hint · COPD with hypercapnia risk: controlled O₂ 88–92% + blood gases”.

cues.text: Read paired results together but know their limits, because low cortisol with high ACTH means the adrenal gland itself has failed, a urea nitrogen to creatinine ratio above 20 is only a weak hint of prerenal injury, and a COPD patient at risk of carbon dioxide retention needs controlled oxygen aimed at saturations of 88 to 92 percent rather than none at all.

props.label: Cortisol ↓ ACTH ↑ = primary · ↓ ↓ = secondary · ↑ ↓ = adrenal · ↑ ↑ = pituitary/ectopic
Ratio > 20 = weak hint · COPD risk: controlled O₂ 88–92% + gases

explanation.what: Plain language: some lab results only make sense in pairs. A stress hormone (cortisol) and the pituitary signal that drives it (ACTH) together show which gland is at fault. Urea and creatinine are both kidney waste markers, and their ratio was long used to guess whether a kidney is just underfilled or damaged, but it works poorly. And in people with severe lung disease who retain carbon dioxide, oxygen is given in measured amounts rather than freely or not at all. Scientific terms: hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal axis, CRH, ACTH, primary and secondary adrenal insufficiency, ACTH-dependent and ACTH-independent Cushing syndrome, Cushing disease, ectopic ACTH, BUN/creatinine ratio, prerenal and intrinsic acute kidney injury, hypercapnic respiratory failure, target saturation, V/Q mismatch, Haldane effect.
explanation.why: Cortisol feeds back on ACTH, so a failing adrenal gland lets ACTH climb, while a failing pituitary leaves both low, and autonomous adrenal cortisol production suppresses ACTH through the same feedback. BUN depends on protein load, catabolism, bleeding, liver function and tubular handling as well as filtration, so the ratio overlaps between causes of kidney injury. Excess oxygen releases hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction and shifts the CO₂ dissociation curve, raising PaCO₂ in patients who cannot increase ventilation.
explanation.measure: Adrenal: low baseline cortisol with raised ACTH can be enough to diagnose primary adrenal insufficiency; cosyntropin stimulation confirms. Cushing: ACTH generally <10 pg/mL = ACTH-independent; >20 pg/mL (normal or elevated) = ACTH-dependent; 5–20 pg/mL gray zone. Ratio: traditional cut-off 20; in studies about half of AKI inpatients exceed it and ROC area was 0.5 in an emergency cohort. Oxygen: 94–98% for most acutely ill adults; 88–92% if at risk of hypercapnia, blood gases within 30–60 min; 24% or 28% Venturi or 1–2 L/min nasal cannulae; move to 94–98% if pH and PCO₂ are normal (unless past hypercapnic failure needing ventilation, or usual saturation <94%).
explanation.differs: Primary vs secondary adrenal insufficiency (ACTH high vs low); ACTH-independent vs ACTH-dependent Cushing syndrome (ACTH suppressed vs normal/high); Cushing disease (pituitary) vs ectopic ACTH; controlled oxygen vs withheld or uncontrolled high-flow oxygen.
explanation.examAngle: Expect: name the disorder from a cortisol–ACTH pair, pick controlled oxygen with a 88–92% target for an at-risk COPD patient, and recognise that a high BUN/creatinine ratio can come from GI bleeding or catabolism rather than prove prerenal azotemia.

mnemonic.text: When the FURNACE (adrenal) breaks, the THERMOSTAT (pituitary ACTH) shouts louder; when the thermostat breaks, both go quiet. A furnace running on its own silences the thermostat. Oxygen is a DIMMER, not an on-off switch: dial it to 88–92. And the BUN/creatinine ratio is a RUMOUR, not a witness.
mnemonic.explanation: Encodes negative feedback in the cortisol–ACTH grid, controlled oxygen, and the weak diagnostic value of the ratio.
mnemonic.limitation: ACTH can fall in a 5–20 pg/mL gray zone; severe illness and stress change how cortisol should be read; the oxygen target becomes 94–98% when blood gases show normal pH and PCO₂ in a patient without past hypercapnic failure.

analogyLimitations: The furnace and thermostat picture ignores CRH, cortisol rhythm and assay limits.
Oxygen targets come from the BTS (UK) guideline; local protocols may differ.
takeaway: Read paired results together but know their limits, because low cortisol with high ACTH means the adrenal gland itself has failed, a urea nitrogen to creatinine ratio above 20 is only a weak hint of prerenal injury, and a COPD patient at risk of carbon dioxide retention needs controlled oxygen aimed at saturations of 88 to 92 percent rather than none at all.

questions.stem: A fatigued patient with darkened skin and hyponatraemia has a low morning cortisol and a high plasma ACTH. The most likely diagnosis is:

options.rationale: Correct. Low cortisol with raised ACTH means the adrenal gland fails despite a strong pituitary signal; hyperpigmentation occurs only in primary disease.

options.text: Secondary adrenal insufficiency from a pituitary lesion
options.rationale: Incorrect. Secondary disease gives a low (not high) ACTH and no hyperpigmentation.
Incorrect. Cushing syndrome means high, not low, cortisol.
Incorrect. Ectopic ACTH drives cortisol up, causing hypercortisolism.

questions.stem: A patient with a COPD exacerbation and previous hypercapnia has SpO₂ 84% on room air. Blood gases are not yet available. The best initial oxygen plan is:

options.text: Controlled oxygen by 24% or 28% Venturi mask, target 88–92%, blood gases within 30–60 minutes
options.rationale: Correct. This matches the BTS approach for patients at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure.

options.text: Withhold oxygen until blood gases confirm the PaCO₂
options.rationale: Incorrect. Oxygen should not be delayed in a seriously ill hypoxaemic patient; it is titrated, not withheld.

options.text: High-flow reservoir mask aiming for 100% saturation
options.rationale: Incorrect. Uncontrolled high-flow oxygen raises the risk of oxygen-induced hypercapnia and acidosis.

options.text: Target 94–98% straight away, as for any acutely ill adult
options.rationale: Incorrect. 94–98% is for patients not at risk; with hypercapnia risk the target is 88–92% until blood gases are reviewed.

questions.stem: A patient with an upper gastrointestinal bleed has BUN 56 mg/dL and creatinine 1.6 mg/dL (ratio 35). Which statement is best supported by the evidence?

options.text: The high ratio may reflect the protein load from bleeding and does not by itself prove prerenal kidney injury
options.rationale: Correct. GI bleeding raises urea production, and studies show the ratio does not reliably separate prerenal from intrinsic AKI.

options.text: A ratio above 20 proves prerenal azotemia
options.rationale: Incorrect. About half of AKI inpatients exceed 20, and in an emergency cohort the ratio had an ROC area of 0.5.

options.text: The ratio proves acute tubular necrosis
options.rationale: Incorrect. The ratio cannot make either diagnosis on its own.
Incorrect. Bleeding into the gut increases urea production, raising the ratio.

Diagnostic performance of serum blood urea nitrogen to creatinine ratio for distinguishing prerenal from intrinsic acute kidney injury in the emergency department. BMC Nephrol. 2017;18(1):173. doi:10.1186/s12882-017-0591-9
references.usedFor: 1103 emergency patients: no significant difference in mean ratio between prerenal and intrinsic AKI, ROC area 0.5 (0.55 in subgroup analyses); non-renal influences raising (GI bleeding, high protein diet, fever, trauma, infection, corticosteroids, tetracycline) and lowering (liver failure, protein malnutrition, osmotic diuresis, acetazolamide) the ratio.

references.citation: Lewis A, Thant AA, Aslam A, Aung PPM, Azmi S. Diagnosis and management of adrenal insufficiency. Clin Med (Lond). 2023;23(2):115-118. doi:10.7861/clinmed.2023-0067
references.usedFor: HPA axis and negative feedback; primary vs secondary definitions; low baseline cortisol with raised ACTH can diagnose primary AI; baseline ACTH distinguishes primary from secondary; autoimmune adrenalitis >70% of primary AI in the Western world; exogenous glucocorticoids suggested as the most common cause of secondary AI; hyperpigmentation in primary only; cosyntropin test; interpret cortisol in light of severe illness; treat adrenal crisis without waiting for tests.

references.citation: Savas M, Mehta S, Agrawal N, van Rossum EFC, Feelders RA. Approach to the Patient: Diagnosis of Cushing Syndrome. J Clin Endocrinol Metab. 2022;107(11):3162-3174. doi:10.1210/clinem/dgac492
references.usedFor: Exogenous corticosteroids are the most common cause of Cushing syndrome; ACTH inappropriately normal or elevated (generally >20 pg/mL) in ACTH-dependent and low (generally <10 pg/mL) in ACTH-independent CS; gray zone 5–20 pg/mL; ACTH-dependent 80–85%; Cushing disease ~80% of ACTH-dependent; ectopic sources such as small-cell lung carcinoma and pulmonary carcinoid.

references.citation: O'Driscoll BR, Howard LS, Earis J, Mak V. British Thoracic Society Guideline for oxygen use in adults in healthcare and emergency settings. BMJ Open Respir Res. 2017;4(1):e000170. doi:10.1136/bmjresp-2016-000170
references.usedFor: Full text read via Europe PMC. Target 94–98% for acutely ill patients not at risk of hypercapnic failure; 88–92% pending blood gases for those at risk; blood gases within 30–60 min; 24% Venturi 2–3 L/min, 28% Venturi 4 L/min or nasal cannulae 1–2 L/min; adjust to 94–98% if pH and PCO₂ normal unless previous hypercapnic failure needing NIV/IPPV or usual saturation <94%; never discontinue or delay oxygen in seriously ill patients; sudden cessation can cause life-threatening rebound hypoxaemia.

references.citation: Abdo WF, Heunks LM. Oxygen-induced hypercapnia in COPD: myths and facts. Crit Care. 2012;16(5):323. doi:10.1186/cc11475
references.usedFor: Full text read via Europe PMC. Reduced respiratory drive is not a major contributor; loss of hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction (V/Q mismatch) accounts for the largest share; Haldane effect about 25% in the cited study; titrated oxygen to 88–92% recommended; withholding oxygen described as unwise.

claims.text: HPA axis, negative feedback; primary vs secondary adrenal insufficiency and their cortisol–ACTH patterns; autoimmune cause, hyperpigmentation, exogenous glucocorticoids.
ACTH-independent (<10 pg/mL, 15–20%) vs ACTH-dependent (normal/high, >20 pg/mL, 80–85%) Cushing syndrome; Cushing disease vs ectopic ACTH; gray zone.
BUN/creatinine ratio theory and cut-off of 20; evidence that it does not separate prerenal from intrinsic AKI; non-renal influences on BUN.
BTS oxygen targets (94–98%; 88–92% with hypercapnia risk), blood gases in 30–60 min, devices, target adjustment, not delaying or abruptly stopping oxygen.
Oxygen-induced hypercapnia mainly from V/Q mismatch and the Haldane effect, with reduced drive a minor contributor.
Reviewer’s “10:1–20:1 ratio = intrinsic renal disease”; cortisol reference values in the Number Vault.
claims.note: Not taught as facts; the 10–20:1 rule is contradicted by Uchino 2012 and Manoeuvrier 2017 (register flag rv-bun-cr-ratio-ch9).

accuracyFlags.issue: Ch. 9 Hit 4 states that a BUN/creatinine ratio >20:1 means prerenal azotemia and that a 10:1–20:1 ratio means intrinsic renal disease. Uchino 2012 (ratio >20 in about half of AKI inpatients, not bimodal, higher mortality with high ratio) and Manoeuvrier 2017 (ROC area 0.5 in 1103 emergency patients) show the ratio does not reliably separate the two (register flag rv-bun-cr-ratio-ch9).

Ch. 9 Hit 9 labels high cortisol + high ACTH as “Cushing disease”. Savas 2022: ACTH-dependent Cushing syndrome includes both Cushing disease (pituitary) and ectopic ACTH, and ACTH may be only inappropriately normal (>20 pg/mL); Lewis 2023 adds that exogenous glucocorticoids are a common cause of low cortisol + low ACTH (register flag rv-acth-dependent-ch9).

Ch. 9 Hit 10 and Trap 6 agree with BTS 2017 on the 88–92% target, but omit that BTS moves the target to 94–98% when blood gases show normal pH and PCO₂ (unless previous hypercapnic failure needing ventilation or usual saturation <94%). Targets come from a UK guideline; local protocols may differ (register flag rv-copd-o2-target-adjust-ch9).
